capabilities.title: Verified simplification
capabilities.summary: Searches a short chain of rewrites toward a goal (simplify, expand, factor, or rewrite in given functions): handbook identities, each at every place it matches and read in either direction, plus SymPy's own moves. Every step is checked at random complex sample points and, separately, with a symbolic zero test; the steps and the identities used are shown. A result that cannot be verified is never shown.
limits: Numerical agreement at sample points is evidence, not proof; only a passed symbolic zero test means SymPy also reduced the difference to zero. Both are reported for every step.

Steps are equalities where both sides are defined. When the result excludes points the input did not (a cancelled factor), it says where it is valid (`x \neq 1`); square-root, logarithm and branch-cut domains are not reported this way.
The search is bounded (at most 4 rewrites in a row, a few alternatives per step, a time budget). "Nothing better was found" does not show that no better form exists.
An identity that matches but whose conditions are not provable from your assumptions is reported with the unmet conditions and never applied.
Symbols are complex unless you declare otherwise, so results that need real or positive symbols are left alone until you say so.
If nothing better is found, the input is returned unchanged and the status says so.
In LaTeX, bare function arguments such as `\sin 2x` and inverse notation such as `\sin^{-1}` are rejected as ambiguous; plain text needs the parentheses, `sin(2*x)`.

capabilities.title: Is this equation an identity?
capabilities.summary: Decides whether one stated equation holds as an identity under the declared assumptions. A true one is reported as proved (the symbolic zero test also found zero) or as numerically checked (no disagreement at random points or at targeted probes: evidence, not proof). A false one is reported with an exact point where the two sides differ, confirmed at 60 and 120 digits. One that is false only because the symbols are complex says which assumption makes it true.
limits: Only a statement the user asked about is judged. In the chat, equations the model writes itself are still never called false (they stay unchecked).
A definition, an equation of motion, a statement about matrices, vectors, distributions or sums is refused, never called true or false; sampling numbers cannot settle it.
Not an identity does not mean no solutions. `x^2 = 4x` is not an identity and has two solutions.

capabilities.title: Verified Taylor series
capabilities.summary: Expands an expression in one variable about a finite real point, to order 12 at most. The coefficients are re-derived from the original function by a contour-integral estimate (no differentiation), and the remainder is measured to shrink at the claimed order. Both checks must pass or no series is shown.
limits: Only Taylor series about a finite point. A pole or branch point at the point (`1/x`, `\sqrt{x}`, `\ln x` at 0) is "unsupported"; Laurent, Puiseux and asymptotic series are not produced.
Functions with no complex derivative (`|x|`) are unsupported.
The error table is a measurement at a few distances for this expression, not a bound.

In the chat, a reply that restates the series as `f(x) = P(x) + O((x-a)^{n+1})` is marked as the tool's result only if the function, the centre, the order and every coefficient agree with it; Big-O notation is otherwise never tested by sampling and stays unchecked. The expansion point and the places where the error was measured are parameters of the call, not definitions the rest of the reply is tested against.

capabilities.title: Approximations
capabilities.summary: Finds a simpler expression that represents a function in the regime you name: Laurent series with pole order and residue, asymptotic expansions at plus or minus infinity, perturbation expansions in a small parameter or a combination such as v/c, Taylor series of several variables with the Hessian, leading behaviour and limits, Padé approximants, Chebyshev and Legendre approximations on an interval, Fourier series of a periodic function, piecewise polynomials, continued fractions of a number, Euler-Maclaurin for a large sum, sequence acceleration, the expansion of an integral, a root or an inverse function in a small parameter, and Laplace's method. `auto` chooses from what you said; `compare` puts Taylor, Padé, Chebyshev and piecewise side by side and picks the simplest that meets an accuracy target. SymPy only proposes: each result is shown only if a check that does not use the route that built it agrees (Cauchy estimates, residual decay at high precision, a second implementation, direct summation, quadrature).
limits: Errors are measured on sampled points and are never bounds; "the tolerance is met" means on the sampled points. A rigorous bound is established only for continued-fraction convergents of a rational.

The interval, point, period, tolerance, degrees and number of modes are yours; none has a default, and a missing one is a question. Taylor and Padé on an interval are expanded about the midpoint only when that is stated.
An asymptotic expansion is not a convergent series, and no term is added "because it should help".

Padé approximants can have poles the function does not have; they are reported. A Padé approximant is not assumed to be more accurate than the Taylor polynomial, and both are measured when an interval is given.
At a jump the Fourier series converges to the midpoint and overshoots by about 9% of the jump (Gibbs); uniform convergence is not claimed. Lanczos sigma factors are optional.
A function with a pole, an undefined point or non-real values on the interval is refused for interval methods. Essential singularities and branch points are not Laurent series and are refused.

Puiseux series, exponentially small or large asymptotics, endpoint and degenerate Laplace maxima, perturbative solutions of differential equations, spherical harmonics and multiscale methods are not covered.

Euler-Maclaurin sums need a smooth summand; an oscillating one is refused when the corrections do not beat the plain integral. A symbolic upper limit is checked for several values, not proved for every N.

capabilities.title: Noncommutative matrix calculus
capabilities.summary: Ordered products of matrix exponentials with declared matrices (a size, or explicit entries), also matrices that depend on a variable, A(t). Minerva recognises the structure and picks the technique: the ordered product rule; the Frechet derivative of exp(X(t)) when X and X' do not commute (never assumed to equal X' exp(X)); merging exponentials only where commutation is declared or visible in the entries; a closed form for an invertible matrix; Duhamel integrals of e^((t-s)A) B e^(sA); a Sylvester equation or a block-matrix exponential for other integrals; and evolution operators dU/dt = A(t) U, U(0) = I. A result is shown only if independent checks agree. An equation, a representation or a numerical approximation is never presented as an evaluated result.
limits: The variable is scalar. A matrix depends on it only if declared (or visible in explicit entries), and A(t) is never read as t times A; integrals of time-dependent matrices are not supported.
Matrices are never assumed to commute (also with their own derivative or at other times) or to be invertible; each must be declared, or be visible in explicit entries.

Time-ordered exponentials, Dyson series and Magnus expansions are not supported. An abstract generator that does not commute with itself at all times is declined; explicit entries with a numeric span are solved numerically.

A numerical solution (up to 4 by 4, double precision) is a measurement on the span you give, checked by a second method, by integrating backwards and by Liouville's formula; the end of the span is a number only you can choose.

Integrals need exponents that are affine in the variable and at most two exponentials depending on it. Abstract matrices give an exact equation or representation, entries only for explicit matrices (at most 4 by 4) whose closed form SymPy finds in time.
The numerical check is evidence, not proof. The exact check compares formal power series through degree 4 and is reported separately.

capabilities.title: Statistical mechanics of explicit systems
capabilities.summary: Builds the partition function of a list of levels, a level family E(n) (finite or infinite), a density of states, a separable classical Hamiltonian, a Hermitian matrix, particles with Bose, Fermi or classical counting, or a periodic chain (transfer matrix), and derives thermodynamic quantities from it by one generic route: differentiate ln Z (or ln Xi) with the other state variables held fixed. Heat capacity is dU/dT, pressure is -dF/dV at fixed temperature, a particle number is a chemical-potential derivative; none is a stored formula. Thermal averages, variances, cumulants and fluctuation-response relations follow, as do microcanonical counts and approximations that report their assumptions, order, validity and a measured error. A formula is shown only if an independent numerical evaluation agreed (direct enumeration with log-sum-exp, adaptive quadrature, matrix exponentials, occupation numbers, brute force over every chain configuration, numerical derivatives); convergence is proved or the request is refused.
limits: An approximation is never an identity. High- and low-temperature expansions, Stirling's ln N! and the thermodynamic limit of a chain are labelled asymptotic and carry a measured error table (a measurement, not a bound); saddle-point and Laplace methods, Legendre transforms and mean field are not supported.

An infinite sum needs a ratio-test proof for every beta > 0 (otherwise `divergent` or `convergence_not_provable`); an integral goes through the verified definite integrator under your assumptions. No interchange of a limit, sum, integral and derivative is assumed.

A classical Hamiltonian must be a sum of one-variable terms; a coupling term is refused (`not_separable`). A matrix is at most 4x4 with closed-form eigenvalues and is never assumed to commute with anything, so a response relation beyond the first derivative, and a covariance, are refused for operators that do not commute. A chain is periodic, with at most three site values, a symmetric bond and at most 14 sites for the brute-force check.

The ensemble is never substituted. Grand canonical needs particles with a statistic (Bose needs mu provably below every level); microcanonical counting needs numeric levels, a number of copies and a total energy that some microstate has, and its comparison with the canonical ensemble is measured, never assumed.

The phase-space cell and whether copies are indistinguishable are your choices, never defaulted; indistinguishable copies use the classical-limit N! counting, not exact Bose or Fermi statistics. Numbers for a numerical evaluation are yours too.

Numerical agreement is evidence, not a proof; a symbolic zero is reported separately and only where SymPy finds one. A series or integral without a closed form is evaluated numerically only and labelled as such.

capabilities.title: Vector calculus in three coordinate systems
capabilities.summary: Gradient, divergence, curl, the scalar and vector Laplacian, dot, cross and triple products, directional derivatives and partial derivatives of scalar and vector fields in Cartesian, cylindrical and spherical coordinates, with fields that are arbitrary functions of position (and time) or given explicitly. Nested operators are supported (up to four). A result is shown only if an independent reading agrees: the input is evaluated directly in Cartesian coordinates by nested finite differences on random smooth fields, sharing no scale factor with the symbolic result. Nothing is assumed smooth: an identity such as curl grad f = 0 needs equal mixed partial derivatives and is withheld until the field is declared twice continuously differentiable. The Jacobian of each system and the conversion of explicit fields between systems are included.
limits: Three orthogonal coordinate systems, physical (orthonormal) components, right-handed frames. No general curvilinear coordinates and no tensor fields (see differential geometry).
Numerical agreement is evidence, not proof. An evaluated result carries no symbolic proof, and the wording says so.
Every symbol must be a coordinate, t, a declared field or a declared constant; an undeclared symbol is refused, never read as a constant.

The axis and origin of curvilinear systems are reported as restrictions. The classical divergence of r-hat over r squared is 0 away from the origin; the `distributional` action derives its delta term for one family only (see below).

`distributional` (three-dimensional delta): one point source of the Coulomb kernel C (r - a)/|r - a|^3 (or the Laplacian of C/|r - a|) with a constant strength and a constant real source, as distributions on R^3. capabilities.title: Derivations in electromagnetism
capabilities.summary: Derivations from the field equations a user adopts as premises (Maxwell's equations in SI units, potentials, statics): the wave equations for the electric and magnetic fields in vacuum, charge conservation, Poynting's theorem, gauge invariance of the fields, Poisson's and Laplace's equations. Each derivation is not a stored answer: its routes are found by the general vector-calculus steps (the handbook's vector identities and the supplied premises) and every identity step is checked by comparing the whole expressions before and after. The result is then evaluated on exact solutions of its premises (plane waves, fields built from random potentials with the sources they imply) and is shown as consistent with them, never as verified by them. A result that used a premise is conditional on it, names it, and is never called an identity or a proof; Minerva does not check that a premise is true. Only the gauge invariance of E and B needs no premise.
limits: Cartesian coordinates, fields depending on x, y, z and t. The checks on exact solutions are not run in other coordinate systems.

Electrostatics with numbers the user gives (field, multipole, boundary_value, check_solution): point charges and a density over a box, Dirichlet problems on a rectangle, Cartesian coordinates. Fourier and Laplace transform methods, retarded Green's functions, finite elements, FDTD and general PDE solving are planned and not implemented.

Seven derivations are available; the wave equations for the potentials in the Lorenz gauge, interface conditions by a pillbox argument and Maxwell's equations in matter with a general constitutive relation are planned, and Minerva says so instead of improvising them.
A premise must match the handbook form exactly; a premise with another sign or form is treated as missing and asked for.
Identities that need equal mixed partial derivatives are applied only to fields the user declared twice continuously differentiable.
The handbook entries for Maxwell's equations are checked for units only (the operators contribute a length or a time); they are premises, not verified laws.

Each step is an operation (simplify, differentiate, integrate, Taylor polynomial) or a handbook identity applied to the previous result, and is verified and saved to your account with what produced it and the assumptions in force. You can continue from any earlier step.
limits: A step is carried forward as its text form, which the parser reads back exactly. A result the text parser cannot read (for example one using `erf` or `Piecewise`) is shown but cannot be continued.

An identity is offered only when the engine reports it applicable (conditions proven from your assumptions); applying it recomputes and re-verifies the rewrite on the server. Handbook entries that are only stated are never applied.
If you edit a carried-forward result, the next step is recorded as a new input, not a continuation.

capabilities.title: Substituting relations
capabilities.summary: Replaces the left side of a relation you supply by its right side, one relation at a time, and records each replacement as a step with the relation it used. The relations are your premises: Minerva checks that the replacement reproduces the original expression, not that your relation is true, so a result that depends on them is shown as holding given them. If the result also holds without them, it says so.
limits: At most four relations, applied once each in the order you give. If another order would give a different result, or the relations rewrite each other, the request is refused until you say whether to apply them in the order listed or all at once; Minerva never picks one.

A relation that can never hold (`x = x + 1`) or relates only numbers is refused. A relation used as a commutation rule (`AB - BA = 1`) is not applied, because only patterns that occur in the expression are replaced.
Replacement finds the occurrences SymPy recognises; a pattern that does not occur leaves the expression unchanged.
The input must be an expression (not an equation). Noncommuting symbols are supported for polynomial expressions, and the order of their factors is kept.
Where a cancelled denominator excludes a point, the result states it (`x \neq 0`).

capabilities.title: Changing one part of an expression
capabilities.summary: Applies one move to one part of an expression and leaves the rest alone: expand, factor, cancel, simplify, collect terms by chosen variables or powers, or a handbook identity. You choose the part from a list the server makes (or type it); if it occurs more than once you choose the occurrence. The whole expression before and after is verified, and an identity whose conditions are not provable from your assumptions is reported and not applied.
limits: A part is chosen for one exact expression; if the expression has changed, the choice is refused as stale and never applied somewhere else.

Rewrite as takes the form you type and verifies the whole expression against the original (numerically, and symbolically where SymPy finds a zero); a form that is not equal is refused. It is not available for noncommuting symbols.
An identity is matched against the chosen part alone, with the same filters as everywhere else (no invented roots, reciprocals or the imaginary unit).

Collect works on symbols and parts of the expression, at most four, and by commuting ones for noncommuting expressions. For noncommuting symbols only expand and collect are supported, on polynomial expressions; every other operation reports that it does not support them.
Verification is numerical, and symbolic where SymPy finds a zero; for noncommuting symbols random matrices sized from the degree are used.

capabilities.title: Solving an equation for one variable
capabilities.summary: Isolates a variable in an equation and lists every solution with the conditions it needs: parameters that must not vanish, values the equation itself excludes, and the parameter values where it degenerates. Polynomial and rational equations are solved in closed form where one exists; a variable that occurs once inside powers, roots, exp and log is solved by undoing each operation, one recorded step at a time. Every solution is substituted back into your equation, and a separate check shows that none was dropped.
limits: Solutions are over the complex numbers. Assumptions on the unknown (real, positive) are not used to choose among them, and the result says so; a logarithm or an exponential gives a family with an integer k_1.

Supported are linear and quadratic factors with symbolic coefficients, cubic and quartic factors with rational coefficients, and one occurrence of the unknown inside sums, products, powers, principal roots, exp and log (a base is accepted only if known positive). Periodic inverses (sin, cos), absolute values, symbolic exponents of the unknown, systems of equations and symbolic polynomials of degree three or more are unsupported, and no partial answer is given.
A root that makes a denominator zero is removed, and a principal root can make a candidate extraneous (the equation √x = -2 has no solution). An equation with no solution is reported as such.
Noncommuting symbols are not supported here.

capabilities.title: Ordinary differential equations
capabilities.summary: Write an equation or a system as you would on paper (y'' + 0.2 y' + y + y^3 = 0, or \frac{d^2 y}{dt^2}). Minerva shows how it read it, describes its structure (order, linearity, autonomy, whether it can be solved for its highest derivative, the equation class) and ranks the approaches that can be tried, with what each needs. You then choose one: a closed form, accepted only after it is substituted back into your equation with derivatives taken numerically; a Taylor series about the point of your initial values; an expansion in a small parameter you name (a regular expansion, or Poincaré–Lindstedt for periodic motion); a numerical solution of an initial-value problem (the integrator, explicit or stiff, is chosen from measured behaviour) or of a boundary-value problem; and, for an autonomous system, its equilibria with their local stability and a phase plane. A numerical result is shown only if an independent integrator agrees, refining the tolerance converges, the integral form of the equation holds and any verified conserved quantity is conserved. A closed form and a numerical run can be compared. Every number (conditions, parameters, the interval, the window, the small parameter) is yours: none is chosen for you.
limits: Ordinary equations and systems only, up to order 10 and 12 first-order states. Partial and delay equations, algebraic constraints, and equations that cannot be solved for their highest derivative (several branches) are refused, never reinterpreted.

A closed form comes from SymPy. Not finding one says nothing about whether one exists, singular solutions are not searched for, and an implicit result or one with an unevaluated integral is labelled as such.

A numerical trajectory is an approximation on the interval you gave, never exact and never valid beyond it. The checks are measurements, not an error bound; stiffness is judged from measured behaviour, not predicted.

A boundary-value solution is one of possibly several (the starting guess that found it is named), and a series is local (its radius of convergence is not determined). Perturbation expansions hold for small values of the parameter and, where a term grows with the variable, only on a bounded interval; multiple scales is not implemented.

Stability is local and from the linearisation. An eigenvalue with zero real part, or parameters without values, leave it undecided; nothing is called globally stable. Equilibria are listed as "found" unless the field is polynomial.

capabilities.summary: Expands the accelerations of a Lagrangian system about an equilibrium the user names, to the order the user asks for. For order 1 this is the linearisation: the matrix of the linear part and, for up to two coordinates without damping, the normal-mode frequencies and eigenvectors. The Euler–Lagrange equations, the equilibrium, each expansion and each frequency are checked independently of SymPy's series, and nothing is shown if one check fails.
limits: The expansion is in all the coordinates at once; it cannot express that only one of several angles is small. That case is a series in the one variable (`series`), or a question.
The result is local to the equilibrium and says nothing about large motions; the sign of a squared frequency is stated only when the declared assumptions decide it.
Normal modes for at most two coordinates and no velocity-linear terms; otherwise the characteristic polynomial. Explicit time dependence and a singular mass matrix are refused.
The time limit is the deployed one (10 s). When the modes do not fit, the verified equations are shown and the result says that the modes were not computed.

capabilities.title: Variational calculus
capabilities.summary: Give an action functional of one or several functions, with derivatives of any order up to four and fixed bounds, and Minerva derives its first variation with every integration by parts listed, the Euler–Lagrange equations (the sum over k of (−1)^k d^k/dt^k of ∂L/∂x^(k)), the complete boundary form, which boundary terms the conditions you declared remove, and the natural boundary conditions. Fixing a value never fixes its derivative, and a condition you did not declare is not assumed. The result is shown only if finite differences of the action itself agree with it. With numbers you supply, it evaluates the action on a trial path or family, verifies the variation along your own path, finds a stationary path by two independent methods, and computes the second variation with honest local diagnostics.
limits: Numerical agreement with finite differences is evidence, not a proof, and the result says so.
Bounds are fixed (no moving endpoints), and the integrand must be smooth (no absolute value, sign or piecewise definitions). Field functionals and partial differential equations are not covered.

A stationary path may be a minimum, a maximum or a saddle, and none is claimed to be unique. A negative direction proves the path is not a minimum; the absence of one among the directions tried proves nothing, and the sufficient conditions (no conjugate points) are not checked.
Stationary paths are found for derivatives up to order two with at most four orders in total, and no unknown may appear without a derivative.

capabilities.title: Creative telescoping for integrals with a parameter
capabilities.summary: For an integral that depends on a parameter, Minerva searches for a differential operator L in the parameter and a certificate G with L f = dG/dx, proves that identity exactly, checks convergence, differentiation under the integral sign and the boundary terms from the assumptions you declare, derives the differential equation of the integral and solves it with independently verified initial values. The relation is discovered, not looked up. A value is shown only if it satisfies the equation exactly, reproduces the initial values and agrees with numerical quadrature of the original integrand; otherwise the proved certificate or the verified equation is returned as a labelled partial result that says what remains unresolved.
limits: The integrand must be a product of rational functions, powers (exponents free of the variable) and exponentials of rational functions, in the variable and the parameter. Sums of such terms, trigonometric functions, logarithms and x**a are refused.
The search is bounded (operator order up to 5, certificate degree up to 12). Finding nothing is reported as "within the searched families" and proves nothing outside them.

Convergence and boundary terms are decided from the declared signs only. A parameter whose sign is not declared gives a certificate and no value; oscillating ends are accepted only through absolute convergence.
The value is checked against quadrature, which is numerical evidence, never called a proof. Full holonomic closure, Ore algebras and hypergeometric summation are not implemented.

capabilities.title: Integration techniques
capabilities.summary: Where SymPy's route does not find a verified integral, a deterministic strategy engine reads the structure of the integrand and tries a few promising techniques: substitution, integration by parts, trigonometric identities, partial fractions, symmetry (parity and King's reflection), Frullani integrals, Schwinger parametrization, differentiation under the integral sign and a numerical estimate. Each candidate is verified against the original integrand by the independent checkers before it is shown, and the answer says which technique produced it, why it applies, its steps and what was checked. No language model takes part in finding or checking a result.
limits: A technique whose conditions are not established is reported as blocked and never applied. Symmetry never gives 0 for an integral whose half-range diverges, and Frullani needs the scales declared positive and finite limits of the function at 0 and infinity.
A definite value is checked by quadrature and is never called proved; an antiderivative is proved only when its derivative simplifies to the integrand.
A numerical estimate is not a formula. Found without being asked it rides along with the unchanged "unsupported" status; it becomes the result only when requested.
Gröbner bases, Lie symmetries, contour integration, principal values and Feynman parameters for several denominators are not covered.

capabilities.title: Find the conserved quantities of a system
capabilities.summary: Give a Lagrangian or a Hamiltonian and ask for its conserved quantities. Minerva derives the equations of motion (confirmed by numerical differentiation), then searches a deterministic ladder of larger and larger families of candidates: polynomials in the velocities or momenta times powers of the coordinates, cos and sin of angles (declared, detected, or cyclic) and powers of t. In each family the conservation condition is solved exactly; a candidate is shown only if it is verified on the equations of motion, and products of what is already known are not counted as discoveries. It then reports which constants are functionally independent (an exact Jacobian rank, with the algebraic relations that tie the rest to them) and exactly which families were and were not searched. You do not choose an ansatz, a power bound or the angles.
limits: Complete within each family searched and nothing more. No additional constant always means within the explored families, never that the system has none.
Only rational equations of motion are searched. Square roots (Cartesian Kepler), logarithms and non-polynomial time dependence are reported as unsupported. At most 3 coordinates.
Families are capped (350 unknown coefficients by default); larger ones are listed as not searched.
Parameters are generic. Constants that exist only at special values (resonant frequency ratios) are found only when those values are given.
Functional independence is a proved lower bound (exact rank at rational points); it is called exact only when an upper bound from the relations meets it. Numerical sampling is never used as proof.
A name such as Runge–Lenz is a recognition the model may offer afterwards; the search never uses it.

capabilities.title: Chat with a model you host
capabilities.summary: A conversation in which a language model plans, asks and explains, and calls the tools above. It runs only when you connect a model, such as one served by Ollama; it is off by default.
limits: The model never computes and never decides correctness. Formulas it writes that no tool produced in the conversation are shown as unchecked. Equations it writes are called false only when the sides differ by a constant; definitions, coordinate changes and equations of motion are not identities, stay unchecked, and are judged only against definitions stated earlier in the conversation.
How well it chooses tools depends on the model, and no model tried so far passes every evaluation case. See docs/model-evaluation.md.
Only Ollama-compatible hosts are supported.

capabilities.title: Read formulas from a photo
capabilities.summary: Attach a photo or screenshot of an equation in the chat. A vision model you host transcribes it to LaTeX, you confirm or correct the transcription, and Minerva's strict parser shows how it reads each formula before anything is computed. capabilities.title: Maximum likelihood, Fisher information and Bayesian updates
capabilities.summary: Derive, from a density, the moments of a family (Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, normal, beta, gamma, Cauchy, uniform), the log-likelihood and score, the maximum-likelihood estimator, the Fisher information and the posterior for a prior. Estimators come from the score equations and are accepted only if the direct log-likelihood has zero slope there, the point lies in the parameter space and the Hessian is negative definite; an optimum is called global only when concavity is proved. Posteriors are found by matching the kernel, never from a table. Independence of observations is never assumed; a likelihood of several observations needs you to state it.
limits: Estimates that lie outside the parameter space for the data (a Bernoulli sample of all zeros, identical normal observations) are declined, not invented.
Families whose support depends on the parameter (uniform on (0, theta)) have no score or information.
The score equations are solved one parameter at a time (triangular systems); moments of the Cauchy family do not exist and are declined.
A prior is your assumption; the posterior holds for it. Only kernels of the supported families are recognised.
Numerical agreement (quadrature, a direct log-likelihood) is evidence, not a proof; the symbolic parts are stated separately.

capabilities.title: Gradients, Jacobians and Hessians of matrix functions
capabilities.summary: Derivatives of scalar functions of vectors and matrices, such as the Gaussian log-likelihood with respect to the mean or the covariance (`-1/2*logdet(S) - 1/2*transpose(x - mu)*inv(S)*(x - mu)`), built by differentials and accepted only if central differences of the original function agree at random real matrices of the declared sizes. Matrices keep their order; the derivative with respect to a symmetric matrix is the gradient within the symmetric matrices (the unconstrained gradient is never returned for it), with the entrywise form labelled separately.
limits: Plain-text syntax only for these actions (`tr`, `det`, `logdet`, `transpose`, `inv`, `*` for the matrix product); `logdet` means log of the absolute determinant.
Over the real numbers (a transpose, not a conjugate transpose); Hermitian and Wirtinger derivatives are not supported.
`inv`, `logdet` and the derivative of `det` need the matrix declared invertible (or positive definite) by you.
Matrix-valued functions have no gradient here (the derivative of a matrix by a matrix is a fourth-order tensor).
The symbolic leg is not run; numerical agreement is evidence, not a proof.
